No text, no answered calls, just a timestamp getting older while I stared at it. She'd switched her phone to airplane mode on the train and fallen asleep, which is the boring answer to most frozen pins. The question I typed into my phone that night was "does airplane mode turn off location tracking?" The answer surprised me. The switch stops your phone sending anything out, and the part that works out where you are keeps running underneath. Most people hit that switch because they want an hour of quiet. Meanwhile the phone keeps listening to satellites and writing down coordinates, and the people who care about you are looking at a map that stopped. Those are two different problems, and they need different fixes. Does airplane mode turn off location tracking? No. Airplane mode cuts everything your phone sends out wirelessly, which means calls, texts, mobile data and, by default, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. The part that works out your position keeps going. Your phone can put itself on the map with zero bars, because satellite positioning never needed your carrier. It's accurate, too. Under the US government's standard for civil satellite positioning, good receivers have been achieving horizontal accuracy of 3 meters or better 95% of the time. Phones do worse indoors or between tall buildings, so treat three meters as the best case, and don't expect it in a parking garage. Even so, on a clear day your phone knows which side of the street you're on, airplane mode or not. [Infographic in Section 2: Diagram showing two-way cellular and Wi-Fi transmissions being blocked by an airplane mode barrier, while one-way GPS satellite signals pass straight down to the phone's receiver unimpeded] Radios talk back, receivers only listen The hardware explains it. Your phone's cellular chip, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth all send as well as receive. They hold conversations with towers, routers and headphones, and those outgoing signals are what airplane mode switches off, so they can't interfere with the plane's radio equipment. GPS works the other way round. The receiver in your phone is like the FM radio in a car. It picks up signals that satellites broadcast whether anyone is listening or not, and it never sends anything back. There's nothing for airplane mode to switch off, so it leaves the receiver alone. What airplane mode does stop is the record your carrier keeps. The US Supreme Court showed how big that record gets in 2018, when it noted that wireless carriers had handed over 12,898 cell-site location points covering 127 days of one man's movements, roughly 101 points a day. That's a location point about every 15 minutes, all day, for four months. Each one was logged because his phone connected to a tower, which it does just by being switched on. Turn on airplane mode and those connections stop for as long as it stays on. The one place you might notice a difference is speed. Without mobile data, your phone can't download the satellite data that usually speeds up its first fix, so it can take longer to lock on. Once it does, the position is as good as ever. Airplane mode cleanly stops the second one. A location-sharing app has no way to reach the internet, so it can't send an update. Your group sees your pin at the last place your phone had data, with a timestamp showing when the connection dropped. That's the dot at the intersection, nine minutes from the apartment, getting older by the minute. The recording keeps going. Walk, drive or run offline with downloaded maps and your navigation app will draw your route on the screen in real time. Fitness apps and the phone's own timeline features save those coordinates to the phone. Take a three-hour train ride in airplane mode and your phone can still log the whole route. Turn airplane mode off, or join the station Wi-Fi, and those records can sync to servers you've never thought about. Phones are chatty when they're connected. A 2021 study by Douglas J. Leith at Trinity College Dublin found that idle phones, barely set up and left untouched, exchanged data with Apple or Google every 4.5 minutes on average, and each connection revealed the phone's IP address. That's about 13 check-ins an hour from a phone sitting on a desk. Airplane mode pauses all of it, and reconnecting sends the backlog. Your group sees that you've paused, not that you've vanished.] Bluetooth, offline finding, and the beacons that outlast a shutdown On current iPhones and Android phones, airplane mode turns Wi-Fi and Bluetooth off by default, then remembers if you turn either one back on. Plenty of people do, usually for headphones or a watch. The airplane icon stays in the status bar while Bluetooth quietly reconnects, and that reopens one of the ways your location can leave the phone. Apple's Find My network uses exactly that route. According to the Apple Platform Security Guide, offline finding is on by default for devices running iOS 13 or later with Find My iPhone enabled, and a disconnected iPhone keeps sending out low-energy Bluetooth signals. Any Apple device that passes by picks up the encrypted signal and sends an approximate location, with a timestamp, back to the owner's account. Your phone doesn't need a connection for any of it. Turning the phone off doesn't end it straight away either. Security researchers from TU Darmstadt, presenting at REcon in 2022, took apart iPhone low-power mode and found that when you shut the phone down, it sends 96 Find My signals at 15-minute intervals, covering a full 24 hours. If the battery has run flat, the signals stop after five hours. In other words, holding down the side button doesn't make an iPhone go silent right away. How to actually stop location tracking on iPhone and Android If you want the phone to stop working out where you are, the setting you need is Location Services. The network switches won't do it. On iPhone, open Settings, tap Privacy and Security, tap Location Services, and switch it off. On Android, open Settings, tap Location, and turn off the main switch. Menu names change a little between versions and brands, so look for the word Location. Switching it off comes at a cost. Turn-by-turn directions stop, rideshare apps can't find you, and emergency calls lose your automatic location. Most people don't want to give that up all day. There's a middle option. Go through your apps one by one and set them to While Using the App, so your maps still work and other apps stop checking where you are when you're not using them. Few people ever open that screen, and if you do, you may find a weather app or a shopping app set to Always. Pew Research Center reported in 2023 that 56% of Americans click agree on privacy policies without reading them, and 61% doubt anything they do will make much difference. On this screen, it does. HeyPolo's general-area sharing lets you show your family a neighborhood-level bubble instead of an exact pin, and your maps keep working.] A frozen pin says the one thing nobody meant to say A young adult who switches on airplane mode to get an evening to themselves is asking for something reasonable. The rest of the family never hears the request. They see a pin that stopped, a battery level that won't update and calls going to voicemail, and they fill the silence with the worst thing they can think of. The 2026 Mott Poll Report from C.S. Mott Children's Hospital found that 52% of US parents of 18- to 25-year-olds use a phone or similar device to see where their child is, and 71% of those have it on all the time. Most of them (95%) say it helps them worry less, and 23% admit it sometimes makes them more anxious. They check most often when their child is out late at night, according to 44% of those parents. In other words, the tool that calms almost every parent makes nearly one in four more anxious some of the time, and mostly late at night. That's when I was staring at that frozen dot at 11:15 pm. The number that explains the airplane mode trick is a different one. Among those same parents, 96% said their child knows about the tracking, but only 54% gave their child the option to opt out. Anyone without an off switch will find one, and the only one on the phone is a blunt tool that takes the whole connection down with it. Families do better when everyone has real controls. HeyPolo's private mode pauses sharing and shows the group it's paused. General-area sharing shows less without going dark. Neither one needs anyone to turn their phone into a brick to get an evening off. The same Mott poll found that 48% of parents say their young adult can see their location too, and in 90% of those families it runs both ways. A lot of families have already worked out that sharing feels fairer when it goes in both directions. Nobody has to negotiate the same boundary twice.] FAQ Can someone track my phone if it's on airplane mode? Not live. A family member or app can't see you moving, because the phone can't send data to the network. Apple's Find My network is the exception. If Bluetooth is switched back on while airplane mode is running, nearby Apple devices can pass an approximate location to the owner's account. What does a location-sharing app show when your phone is in airplane mode? Your last known location, with the time your phone last had a mobile or Wi-Fi connection. Your group sees you as offline or paused, and nothing updates until you reconnect. Can 911 find me if my phone is on airplane mode? Calling 911 overrides airplane mode on current iPhone and Android phones and reconnects to the nearest tower. How accurate your location is depends on the phone, the terrain and the local dispatch center, so it isn't guaranteed to be precise. What you lose is new map data. Without a connection, the app can't download new areas, so download your maps before you go offline. Does turning off location services save battery compared to airplane mode? Airplane mode saves more. The mobile radio uses a lot of power keeping in touch with distant towers, so switching it off makes the bigger difference. The GPS receiver only uses a modest amount while it's working out your position. Does turning on airplane mode notify your family group? No. Location-sharing apps, including HeyPolo, don't send a message when you switch on airplane mode. Your group just sees you go offline and your pin stop updating.
